Write $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ and $\|x\|_2=(x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2)^{1/2}$ for $x\in\mathbb R^3$. For $\alpha=(\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3)\in\mathbb N_0^3$, exponent $a>0$, and center $A\in\mathbb R^3$, a **primitive Cartesian Gaussian** is
$$g_{\alpha,a,A}(x)=\prod_{j=1}^3(x_j-A_j)^{\alpha_j}\exp(-a\|x-A\|_2^2),\qquad x\in\mathbb R^3.$$
A **finite Gaussian contraction** is a finite sum $\phi=\sum_{k=1}^q c_k g_{\alpha_k,a_k,A_k}$ with $q\in\mathbb N_0$, $c_k\in\mathbb C$, $a_k>0$, and $A_k\in\mathbb R^3$. The zero-term sum is the zero function. Bras are conjugated.

For a pair of contractions put $f_{\phi,\psi}(x)=\overline{\phi(x)}\psi(x)$. For pair densities $f,g$, define the **Coulomb form**
$$\mathcal C(f,g)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\overline{f(x)}g(y)}{\|x-y\|_2}\,dy\,dx.$$
For finite contractions $\phi,\psi,\rho,\sigma$, define the overlap, kinetic, point-nucleus attraction, and two-electron Coulomb expressions by
$$S(\phi,\psi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{\phi(x)}\psi(x)\,dx,\qquad T(\phi,\psi)=-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^3}\overline{\phi(x)}\,\Delta\psi(x)\,dx,$$
$$V_C(\phi,\psi)=\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{\overline{\phi(x)}\psi(x)}{\|x-C\|_2}\,dx,$$
$$G(\phi,\psi;\rho,\sigma)=\mathcal C(f_{\phi,\psi},f_{\rho,\sigma}).$$
The primitives and their finite contractions are smooth: [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] supplies smoothness of exp, and repeated coordinatewise applications of [[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]] supply all polynomial-product and composition derivatives. Thus the following Laplacian is well defined.

Here $\Delta\psi=\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_{x_j}^2\psi$ is the Cartesian Laplacian.
All displayed integrals mean Lebesgue integrals in the sense of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. A finite nuclear attraction is any finite real linear combination of the $V_C$ terms, with its centers and weights specified. This definition alone asserts neither convergence nor a physical approximation postulate.

derivations.claim: Since $p=a+b>0$, expand the left exponent using $\|x-A\|^2=\|x\|^2-2A\cdot x+\|A\|^2$. The quadratic and linear terms agree with $p\|x-P\|^2$ because $pP=aA+bB$. The remaining constant satisfies $$a\|A\|^2+b\|B\|^2-p\|P\|^2=\frac{ab}{p}\|A-B\|^2=\mu\|A-B\|^2,$$ by substituting $P=(aA+bB)/p$ and expanding the inner products. Thus $a\|x-A\|^2+b\|x-B\|^2=p\|x-P\|^2+\mu\|A-B\|^2$, which gives the exponential identity.

Each coordinate obeys $x_j-A_j=(x_j-P_j)+(P_j-A_j)$ and $x_j-B_j=(x_j-P_j)+(P_j-B_j)$. The finite binomial theorem expands each integer power as a polynomial in $x_j-P_j$ of no larger degree; multiplying the six coordinate polynomials gives a finite polynomial of total degree at most $|\alpha|+|\beta|$.
The coefficients $a/p$ and $b/p$ are positive and sum to one. Hence $P$ is a convex combination of $A$ and $B$, so it lies on their closed line segment, including the case $A=B$.

$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

derivations.claim: The integrand in [F1] is positive for every real $T$; when $T\ge0$ it is at most $t^{2m}$, whose integral is $1/(2m+1)$. Setting $T=0$ gives equality. By [F9], on a compact parameter interval $[-M,M]$ the exponential-series partial sums converge pointwise on $[0,1]$ and are bounded in absolute value by $e^M$; [F7] therefore permits integration term by term and gives the displayed series. For a fixed $T$, choose $M>|T|+1$ and $|h|<1$. By [F8] and the chain rule, the difference quotient of $e^{-Tt^2}$ in $T$ is $-t^2e^{-\xi t^2}$ for some $\xi$ between $T$ and $T+h$, so after multiplication by $t^{2m}$ it is bounded by $e^M t^{2m+2}$. Dominated convergence [F7] passes the difference-quotient limit through the integral and gives $F'_m(T)=-F_{m+1}(T)$.

On $[0,1]$, integrate by parts [F6] with $u(t)=t^{2m+1}$ and $v'(t)=-2Tt e^{-Tt^2}$, so $v(t)=e^{-Tt^2}$. The boundary increment is $e^{-T}$, while the two integrals are $-2TF_{m+1}(T)$ and $-(2m+1)F_m(T)$. Rearranging gives $2TF_{m+1}=(2m+1)F_m-e^{-T}$.

For $T>0$, use the increasing surjection $t=\sqrt{u/T}$ from $(0,T]$ to $(0,1]$. Its derivative is continuous on compact truncations away from zero, as are the integrands, so the proper substitution hypotheses of [F5] hold there. Then $dt=\frac12T^{-1/2}u^{-1/2}du$ and $t^{2m}=T^{-m}u^m$, giving $\gamma(m+\tfrac12,T)/(2T^{m+1/2})$ on passage to the zero endpoint. The original integrand is bounded there, and the transformed one is bounded by a constant times $u^{m-1/2}$, whose exponent is greater than $-1$; both improper integrals therefore converge.

In [F2], substitute $u=x^2$ for $\Gamma(1/2)$. This is an increasing differentiable surjection of $(0,\infty)$ onto itself, with continuous derivative and continuous integrands on compact truncations away from zero; hence [F5] applies separately at zero and infinity. The transformed integrand is $2e^{-x^2}$, integrable at both ends by [F3], so symmetry gives $\Gamma(1/2)=2\int_0^\infty e^{-x^2}dx=\sqrt\pi$. Repeated use of [F4] gives $\Gamma(m+\tfrac12)=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(j+\tfrac12)\sqrt\pi$. Multiplying the odd factors yields $(2m)!/(4^m m!)$, proving the half-integer formula, including the empty product when $m=0$.

Let $n,r\ge1$ be integers, $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}$, $D\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$, $H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, and $G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n\times n\times n}$. Define their transformed tensors by
$$H'_{pq}=\sum_{a,b=1}^n C_{ap}H_{ab}C_{bq},\qquad G'_{pqrs}=\sum_{a,b,c,d=1}^n C_{ap}C_{bq}C_{cr}C_{ds}G_{abcd},$$
for $1\le p,q,r,s\le r$. Define the finite **variational energy functional**
$$E(C;D,H,G)=\sum_{p,q=1}^r D_{pq}H'_{pq}+\frac12\sum_{p,q,r,s=1}^r D_{pq}D_{rs}G'_{pqrs}.$$
Its gradient $\nabla_C E$ is the ordinary Euclidean gradient with respect to the $nr$ real entries of $C$. The basis dimension is $n$, the contracted dimension is $r$, and for any finite matrix or tensor $A$, $\|A\|_F=(\sum |A_{i_1\ldots i_k}|^2)^{1/2}$, with the sum over all its entries. This is a finite algebraic functional; it assumes no Hartree–Fock, self-consistency, or minimizing-state postulate.

For perturbed integral tensors $\widetilde H,\widetilde G$, write $\widetilde E$ for the same functional with those tensors and the same fixed $C,D$. The word “variational” here names the finite coefficient functional only; no claim about a stationary point or physical energy is included.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

derivations.claim: Apply [F2] to each column $c_p$ of $C$: $\|c_p\|_1\le\sqrt n\|c_p\|_2\le\sqrt nB$. Therefore every transformed one-body error satisfies $|\Delta H'_{pq}|\le\varepsilon_2\|c_p\|_1\|c_q\|_1\le nB^2\varepsilon_2$. With $r^2$ entries, $\|\Delta H'\|_F\le rnB^2\varepsilon_2$.

Each transformed four-index error is bounded by $\varepsilon_4\prod_{j\in\{p,q,r,s\}}\|c_j\|_1\le n^2B^4\varepsilon_4$. There are $r^4$ entries, so $\|\Delta G'\|_F\le r^2n^2B^4\varepsilon_4$. The rank-two coefficient tensor $(D_{pq}D_{rs})$ has Frobenius norm $\|D\|_F^2\le M^2$.

For a fixed entry $C_{a\mu}$, differentiating the two occurrences of $C$ in $H'$ yields two sums. Each row of $D$ or column of $D$ has $\ell^1$ norm at most $\sqrt rM$ by [F2], while $\sum_b|\Delta H_{ab}||C_{bq}|\le\sqrt nB\varepsilon_2$. Thus each gradient entry from $H$ has magnitude at most $2\sqrt{nr}BM\varepsilon_2$, and the Frobenius norm over $nr$ entries is at most $2nrBM\varepsilon_2$.

Differentiating the four factors of $C$ in $G'$ gives four sums. For each fixed slot, the sum over the other three basis indices is at most $n^{3/2}B^3\varepsilon_4$ by [F2]. The remaining coefficient sum over the three orbital indices is at most $r^{3/2}M^2$: one row or column of $D$ has $\ell^1$ norm at most $\sqrt rM$ and all entries of the other copy sum to at most $rM$. Including the factor $1/2$ and four slots, each gradient entry is bounded by $2n^{3/2}r^{3/2}B^3M^2\varepsilon_4$. Multiplying by $\sqrt{nr}$ for its $nr$ entries gives $2n^2r^2B^3M^2\varepsilon_4$.

By finite Cauchy–Schwarz, the one-body energy error is at most $\|D\|_F\|\Delta H'\|_F\le MrnB^2\varepsilon_2$. Pairing $(D_{pq}D_{rs})$ with $\Delta G'$ gives the two-body bound $\tfrac12M^2r^2n^2B^4\varepsilon_4$. Adding them proves the energy estimate.
The full gradient error is the sum of the one-body and two-body gradient errors. The triangle inequality and steps 1.3 and 1.4 give the claimed bound.

Let $a,b>0$, $A,B\in\mathbb R^3$, $p=a+b$, $\mu=ab/p$, and $P=(aA+bB)/p$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\exp(-a\|x-A\|_2^2)\exp(-b\|x-B\|_2^2)=\exp(-\mu\|A-B\|_2^2)\exp(-p\|x-P\|_2^2).$$
For any multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^3$, the polynomial factor $(x-A)^\alpha(x-B)^\beta$ is a finite polynomial in $x-P$ of total degree at most $|\alpha|+|\beta|$. Moreover, $P=(a/p)A+(b/p)B$ lies on the closed segment from $A$ to $B$.

Using $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ from [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], for $p>0$, $P\in\mathbb R^3$, and $t,u,v\in\mathbb N_0$, the **Hermite Gaussian** is
$$\Lambda_{tuv}(x;p,P)=\frac{\partial^{t+u+v}}{\partial P_1^t\partial P_2^u\partial P_3^v}\exp(-p\|x-P\|_2^2).$$
For $\eta>0$, $P,C\in\mathbb R^3$, and $n,t,u,v\in\mathbb N_0$, define the **Boys Coulomb auxiliary function**
$$R^n_{tuv}(\eta,P-C)=(-2\eta)^n\frac{\partial^{t+u+v}}{\partial P_1^t\partial P_2^u\partial P_3^v}F_n\!\left(\eta\|P-C\|_2^2\right).$$
Each derivative is an ordinary derivative of a smooth real function of the displayed center coordinates. For the Gaussian this follows from [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and repeated coordinatewise product and chain rules in [[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]]. For the Boys composition, [[thm-boys-integral-identities-series-and-incomplete-gamma]] gives $F_n^{(k)}(T)=(-1)^kF_{n+k}(T)$ by iteration on the full real extension; these derivatives are continuous by its integral representation and compact-uniform domination. The chain rules therefore also apply when $P=C$, where the Boys argument is zero. The multi-index $(t,u,v)$ records derivative order and $n$ records Boys order; both are nonnegative integers.

derivations.claim: Repeated product-rule differentiation shows that every fixed spatial or primitive-parameter derivative of a Gaussian factor is a finite sum of polynomial-Gaussian terms. On the compact parameter sets in the Statement, choose $0<a_0\le a\le a_1<\infty$ and $\|A\|\le R$. The coefficients of these finitely many polynomials are bounded uniformly, since they are polynomials in the bounded parameters. Moreover, $\|x-A\|^2\ge\tfrac12\|x\|^2-\|A\|^2$ and $e^{-a\|x-A\|^2}\le e^{-a_0\|x-A\|^2}\le e^{a_0R^2}e^{-a_0\|x\|^2/2}$. Each term is therefore bounded by $K(1+\|x\|)^N e^{-a_0\|x\|^2/2}$ for finite $K,N$ uniform on those parameter sets. This majorant is integrable by [F2] and bounded, so each pair product is in $L^1\cap L^\infty$; products involving $\Delta\psi$ have the same form. For fixed parameters use singleton compact sets.

The overlap and kinetic integrands are polynomial-Gaussian products and are absolutely integrable by step 1.1. For a nuclear center $C$, the pair product is bounded on $\|x-C\|<1$. To check local kernel integrability without a radial-coordinate formula, partition $0<\|z\|<1$ into $A_k=\{2^{-(k+1)}\le\|z\|<2^{-k}\}$: on $A_k$, $\|z\|^{-1}\le2^{k+1}$ and $A_k$ lies in a cube of volume $8\cdot2^{-3k}$, so $\int_{A_k}\|z\|^{-1}dz\le16\cdot4^{-k}$. The sum is $64/3$. Outside this unit ball the kernel is at most one, so the remaining integral is bounded by the pair product's $L^1$ norm. This proves absolute convergence of the point-nucleus attraction.

Let $f,g$ be two pair products from finite contractions; by step 1.1 they belong to $L^1\cap L^\infty$. On $\|x-y\|<1$, Tonelli [F3] and $z=y-x$ give the bound $\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty\int_{\|z\|<1}\|z\|^{-1}dz\le(64/3)\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty$ by the shell calculation in step 2.1. On the complement, $\|x-y\|^{-1}\le1$, giving bound $\|f\|_1\|g\|_1$. Hence the two-electron integrand is absolutely integrable, and [F4] supplies its product and iterated integral meanings.

Primitive-center and exponent derivatives only increase the polynomial degrees of the Gaussian factors; the singular centers $C$ and diagonal $x=y$ are fixed. The near-nucleus and near-diagonal estimates in steps 2.1 and 3.1 therefore apply uniformly to their difference quotients: [L8] bounds each quotient by the corresponding next parameter derivative, whose compact-uniform Gaussian majorant is given in step 1.1. Applying [F5] passes each derivative through the integral. Finite linearity extends every result from primitives to contractions.

By [F2], the absolute Coulomb integrand is integrable; Tonelli [F5] on its nonnegative product with the $s$-integral therefore permits insertion of the Laplace representation into $\mathcal C(f,f)$.

At $s=0$ the double integral equals $|\int f|^2\ge0$; for $s>0$, factor $$e^{-s^2\|x-y\|^2}=e^{-s^2\|x\|^2}e^{-s^2\|y\|^2}\prod_{j=1}^3e^{2s^2x_jy_j}.$$ Expanding the three exponentials gives terms $(2s^2)^{|\alpha|}x^\alpha y^\alpha/\alpha!$. The pointwise absolute sum after multiplying the Gaussian factors is at most one, because $\sum_j|x_jy_j|\le\|x\|\|y\|$ by [F6] and $\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2-2\|x\|\|y\|=(\|x\|-\|y\|)^2\ge0$. Its product with $|f(x)||f(y)|$ is integrable, with double integral at most $\|f\|_1^2$. Tonelli and Fubini [F5] therefore permit termwise integration and factor each term, yielding $$\int\int\overline{f(x)}f(y)e^{-s^2\|x-y\|^2}\,dy\,dx=\sum_{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3}\frac{(2s^2)^{|\alpha|}}{\alpha!}\left|\int f(x)x^\alpha e^{-s^2\|x\|^2}\,dx\right|^2\ge0.$$

Input a nonnegative integer $M$, a finite dyadic interval $\mathcal T=[T_-,T_+]\subset[0,\infty)$, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, a finite integer work cap $W$, a finite integer precision cap $P\ge2$, and a dyadic format with precision $2\le p\le P$, exponent bounds and elementary truncation index $K\ge1$. These are the backend parameters of [[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]]. The output is a table of real dyadic intervals $I_m$ for $0\le m\le M$, with status `success`, `inconclusive`, `domain`, or `range`.

All arithmetic uses [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]. Every real elementary call means a typed DAG call to [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] at the supplied format and fixed $K$. Embed an exact rational argument by outward rounding; check the domain of the entire rounded argument before calling. Square roots use the outward square-root operation. No machine elementary value is an endpoint certificate. Maintain a shared work counter: charge each arithmetic operation, conversion, comparison, loop update, summand and primitive child operation before executing it. Interrupt a child when the remaining counter reaches zero. A cap exhaustion, unresolved enclosure test, intermediate overflow, or child non-success on otherwise valid data makes the affected seed or directional candidate unavailable; if no candidate succeeds, return `inconclusive`. Return `range` only when a certified bound proves that an exact requested table value lies outside the largest finite magnitude of the supplied format. Invalid original inputs give `domain`; a domain test obscured only by intermediate rounding gives `inconclusive`.

1. Validate the stated input conditions and supported format. Process the distinct endpoints in increasing order; process the distinct seed orders $m\in\{0,M\}$ in increasing order. At an endpoint $\tau=0$, form the exact rationals $1/(2m+1)$ for every $0\le m\le M$. If any exact value exceeds the largest finite magnitude of the format, return `range`; otherwise round the rationals outward to the output format. Use this table without a recurrence. A rational is retained exactly internally, but a non-dyadic rational is not returned as a singleton dyadic interval.

2. For each positive endpoint $\tau$, perform refinements $k=0,1,\ldots,W-1$, subject to the shared work counter. At refinement $k$, try the two seed orders separately using their own $m$ and $s=m+\tfrac12$:

   - If $0<\tau\le1$, evaluate the Taylor polynomial through $N=k$ from [[thm-boys-integral-identities-series-and-incomplete-gamma]], then enlarge by the outward upper bound for $\tau^{N+1}/((N+1)!(2m+2N+3))$ from [[lem-boys-small-taylor-remainder]]. The condition $N+2\ge\tau$ holds throughout this branch.
   - If $1<\tau\le2m+1$, use $N=2^k$ panels of [[lem-boys-positive-midpoint-enclosure]], in increasing node order $j=1,\ldots,N$, and enlarge the positive midpoint sum by $(m+\tau)/(2N)$. Its dyadic nodes are formed exactly before storage; evaluate their exponentials by the finite real elementary call.
   - If $\tau>2m+1$, request the Gamma target from [[alg-certified-gamma-loggamma-evaluation]] on the exact rectangle $[s,s]+i[0,0]$, with child absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a/2^{k+2}$, no relative request, base format precision $p_0=p$, the same exponent bounds and fixed elementary truncation $K$, child precision cap $P$, and child work cap $w=\lfloor R/4\rfloor$, where $R$ is the remaining parent work at call entry. If $w<1$, stop `inconclusive`. Debit its actual work, including unsuccessful work, to the parent counter. A successful child rectangle has real projection containing the real number $\Gamma(s)$: its reality follows from the positive-real Euler integral, also evaluated by the half-integer identity in [[thm-boys-integral-identities-series-and-incomplete-gamma]]. Use this projection as the real Gamma enclosure. Evaluate $e^{-\tau}$ by the real elementary call, and use [[lem-boys-incomplete-gamma-large-t-tail-bound]] to form the enclosing interval for $F_m(\tau)$. Compute $\tau^s=\tau^m\sqrt\tau$ and $\tau^{s-1}=\tau^s/\tau$ by outward operations; the exact denominator $1-\max(s-1,0)/\tau$ is positive. Replace a negative lower endpoint by zero, retaining the upper endpoint. A child `range`, a child `domain` on this valid positive argument, or a child `inconclusive` invalidates that seed attempt and permits the next bounded refinement; no child status is propagated as a range claim for the Boys output.

   A finite seed interval is available to its direction only when its radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. A failed attempt does not invalidate a successfully enclosed seed for the other direction. Every panel and child loop is subject to the counter, even when its formal index bound is very large.

3. At each refinement obtain one finite real interval $J$ for $e^{-\tau}$. From an available order-zero seed form the upward candidate for orders $0,\ldots,M$; from an available order-$M$ seed form the downward candidate for orders $M,\ldots,0$. Use the exact affine recurrence maps in [[lem-boys-upward-downward-recurrence-error-amplification]]: compute each affine image's endpoints by exact rational endpoint arithmetic, then convert those two endpoints outward once. If either conversion overflows, discard that directional candidate at this refinement. Otherwise record the two conversion errors and propagate the lemma's radius bounds, including half their sum at each step. This prescription avoids omitting rounding at intermediate nodes. A table is admissible only if every entry satisfies the propagated bound and the requested absolute and, if requested, zero-excluding relative-radius test. Keep the admissible candidate with smaller maximum radius, ties upward. If neither direction is admissible, continue to the next refinement. Once an endpoint table is chosen, proceed to the next endpoint. No upward division is attempted at zero.

4. With both endpoint tables, form $I_m=\operatorname{hull}(I_m(T_+),I_m(T_-))$ for every requested order, using endpoint minima and maxima. By $F'_m(T)=-F_{m+1}(T)<0$ from [[thm-boys-integral-identities-series-and-incomplete-gamma]], this encloses the full range over $\mathcal T$. Return `success` only after every output radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$ and, when relative tolerance is requested, the interval excludes zero and satisfies the relative-radius test in [[def-certified-evaluation-result-contract]]. At a positive endpoint, return `range` only if a certified lower bound for some requested exact Boys value exceeds the largest finite magnitude of the format; a merely overflowing enclosure endpoint gives `inconclusive`. radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.

exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants

fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has

- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.

  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

$\Gamma$, call the complex exponential node on the selected rectangle and
use its finite output rectangle. Return success at the first stage whose
candidate radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. Set relative_certified to true
exactly when relative tolerance was requested, zero is excluded, and the
contract's relative-radius test passes; a failed relative test does not
prevent absolute success. If no stage succeeds before its caps, return
inconclusive.

For any finite dyadic rectangle $Z\subset\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$,
whenever [[alg-certified-gamma-loggamma-evaluation]] returns `success`, its
returned enclosure contains the range of $\Gamma$ or the continued log-Gamma
branch on $Z$ and passes the stated absolute-radius test. Any reported
relative certificate obeys the zero-exclusion condition. No assertion
guarantees success for every valid input or finite cap. Every execution with
finite caps terminates.

Input: a finite, well-formed, typed expression DAG with one or more designated
output nodes; finite real interval or complex rectangle assignments for its
input nodes; exact dyadic constants or constants supplied with certified
enclosing intervals/rectangles; a finite dyadic format $(p,e_{\min},e_{\max})$
with $p\ge2$ and $e_{\min}\le e_{\max}$; and an integer truncation index
$N\ge1$. Input interval endpoints and supplied constant enclosures use this
format. All constants, including every Machin enclosure of $\pi$, use the
same fixed $N$ and format throughout a call. Real nodes support input and
constant nodes and the operations $+,-,\times,\div,\sqrt{\phantom{x}},
\exp,\ln,\arctan,\sin,\cos,\tan$. Complex nodes support input and constant
nodes and $+,-,\times,\div,\exp,\operatorname{Log}$. Each operation has
homogeneous real or complex inputs of its stated type; no implicit conversion
between real and complex nodes is performed. Unsupported node types, arities,
or type combinations return `inconclusive` with the offending node.

Output: a finite interval/rectangle enclosure for every designated output
node, or one of `empty`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `split-domain`, `overflow`,
or `inconclusive` with the node and unresolved domain piece. If any supplied
input is `empty`, return `empty`. No value from a system `libm` routine is
treated as a certified endpoint. Each DAG node is evaluated once; shared nodes
reuse their interval/rectangle enclosure and do not preserve correlations
between distinct paths.

1. Check that node identifiers are unique, all references resolve, every
designated output is a node, and the supported node types and arities above
hold. Use each supplied input enclosure as its node value. For an exact real
dyadic constant $c$, use $[\operatorname{rd}(c),\operatorname{ru}(c)]$ in the
selected format. For an exact complex dyadic constant, do this to each
coordinate. A finite subnormal endpoint remains a valid endpoint; if a
coordinate conversion overflows, return `overflow` with that constant node.
Use a supplied certified constant enclosure as given. Construct a topological
order by repeatedly removing a node whose
predecessors have already been removed, breaking ties by lexicographically
smallest node identifier. If no such node exists before all nodes are ordered,
return `inconclusive` with a node in the cycle. Evaluate nodes in this order
and store each finite enclosure for its successors. Arithmetic nodes use
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; if an operation returns
a non-finite status, propagate it immediately with its node and unresolved
piece. For $\sqrt{X}$ require $X\subseteq[0,\infty)$ and for $\ln X$ require
$X\subseteq(0,\infty)$; otherwise return `domain-error` rather than silently
discarding points.

2. For a real exponential node, set $s=\max(0,e_{\max}+2)$ using the format
in [[def-dyadic-floating-point-format-and-directed-rounding]]. Since
$N_{\max}<2^{e_{\max}+1}$, exact comparison gives $N_{\max}/2^s<1/2$. For
its input interval $X$, form the exact dyadic interval $U=2^{-s}X$
without storage rounding. Evaluate the degree-$N$ exponential polynomial and
add the symmetric tail from
[[lem-range-reduced-exp-log-and-arctan-series-enclosures]], using
$\max_{u\in U}|u|<1/2$, by exact rational interval arithmetic. Round only
the resulting interval endpoints outward, then square that interval $s$ times. If its lower
endpoint is not positive or an endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the node and input interval.

For a real logarithm node, first require $X\subseteq(0,\infty)$. List all
integers $j$ for which $X_j=X\cap[2^j,2^{j+1}]$ is nonempty; exact endpoint
comparisons find this finite list because $X$ has positive finite endpoints.
On each piece form $Y=2^{-j}X_j\subseteq[1,2]$ and $V=(Y-1)/(Y+1)$
by exact rational endpoint formulas without storage rounding, so
$V\subseteq[0,1/3]$. Evaluate the logarithm polynomial and its tail
determined by $\max|V|$ by exact rational interval arithmetic, round the
result outward, and form $j\ln2+\ln Y$ by outward arithmetic. Compute the fixed enclosure for
$\ln2$ once by the same series and tail at $y=2$, hence $v=1/3$, and reuse it
in every bin. If any piece cannot be evaluated finitely, propagate its status
and that piece. Otherwise take the interval hull of all piece enclosures as
the node enclosure.

3. Partition a real arctangent input at the fixed breakpoints
$-3,-1,-1/2,1/2,1,3$ into nonempty closed pieces, allowing shared endpoints.
On pieces in $[-1/2,1/2]$, evaluate its alternating power series. For positive
pieces in $[1/2,1]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4-\arctan((1-t)/(1+t))$; in $[1,3]$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/4+\arctan((t-1)/(t+1))$; for $t\ge3$, use
$\arctan t=\pi/2-\arctan(1/t)$. Evaluate negative pieces by odd symmetry. Form each reduced interval by
exact rational endpoint formulas and evaluate its polynomial and symmetric
tail by exact rational interval arithmetic before outward conversion; every
reduced argument lies in $[-1/2,1/2]$. Combine the converted enclosure with
the fixed $\pi$ enclosure by outward arithmetic. Enclose $\pi$ using Machin's identity and the alternating series at $1/5$ and
$1/239$, forming rational partial sums and tail endpoints exactly before
final outward conversion. If every piece is finite, take the interval hull of
all piece enclosures. If any branch test or piece is unresolved, return its
non-finite status with that piece and do not use a partial hull.

4. For each sine or cosine node, first compute one outward Machin interval
$P_N$ for $\pi$ using the same $N$ and format, combining the rational series
endpoints exactly before final outward conversion. If $P_N$ is non-finite or
its lower endpoint is not positive, return `inconclusive`. For finite input
$X=[a,b]$, put $M_X=\max(|a|,|b|)$, $p_-:=\inf(P_N)>0$, and
$K=\lceil2M_X/p_-\rceil+1$, with the ceiling computed by exact rational
comparisons. If the width of $X$ is at least $2\sup(P_N)$, outward-round the
exact endpoints $-1$ and $1$; if either conversion overflows, return
`overflow` with the node and input interval, and otherwise return the resulting
interval. Otherwise examine the finite candidate list $k=-K,\ldots,K$ for
the canonical cells $[k\pi/2-\pi/4,k\pi/2+\pi/4]$. For each candidate form
the exact rational interval enclosure
$C_k=kP_N/2+[-1/4,1/4]P_N$ of its canonical cell. For $k>K$, the exact
left endpoint $(2k-1)\pi/4$ of cell $k$ is at least
$(2k-1)p_-/4>M_X$; for $k<-K$, its exact right endpoint
$-(2|k|-1)\pi/4$ is at most $-(2|k|-1)p_-/4<-M_X$. Thus no omitted exact
cell can intersect $X$. Include each candidate whose $C_k$ intersects $X$;
exclude only candidates whose intersection is empty by exact comparison. Let
$X_k$ be the exact interval hull of $X\cap C_k$, without rounding these
endpoints, and form the residual enclosure $R_k=X_k-kP_N/2$. Certify
$R_k\subseteq[-1,1]$, evaluate the sine polynomial through degree $2N+1$ or
the cosine polynomial through degree $2N$, and add the corresponding explicit
geometric tail from [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]]
by exact rational interval arithmetic. For $j\in\{0,1,2,3\}$ the
quarter-period map for a sine node is respectively
$\sin r,\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r$, and for a cosine node it is respectively
$\cos r,-\sin r,-\cos r,\sin r$, where $j$ is the least nonnegative residue
of $k$ modulo $4$. For a negative sign, negate the interval and reverse its
endpoints. Intersect each mapped enclosure with $[-1,1]$. Round the final
endpoints outward and take the hull over every included cell.
If no candidate is included, a cell cannot be certified in the reduced
interval, or any candidate endpoint overflows, return `inconclusive` or
`overflow` with the cell; never omit that piece from a finite hull.

For tangent, form the same finite canonical-cell list even when the input width
meets the wide-input shortcut; do not use that shortcut. For each included cell
$k$, form its reduced input interval $R_k$ as above and evaluate sine and
cosine on that cell. Divide their enclosures only when the cosine enclosure
excludes zero. Otherwise, for odd $k$, form the exact dyadic pole enclosure
$K_k=kP_N/2$. If $K_k$ is contained in the cell's input intersection, then
$k\pi/2$ lies in that cell and is a cosine zero, so return `split-domain` with
the cell. If the cosine enclosure contains zero but this pole test does not
certify a zero, return `inconclusive` with the cell. Take the interval hull of
tangent enclosures only when every piece is finite.

5. For complex exponential on $X+iY$, evaluate real $\exp(X)$, $\cos(Y)$,
and $\sin(Y)$ and combine their enclosures by rectangle operations. For
principal $\operatorname{Log}$, first require a rectangle excluding zero and
every point of the negative real branch cut; otherwise return `domain-error`.
Compute an outward Machin interval $P_N$ for $\pi$ using this call's $N$ and
format; if it is non-finite or its lower endpoint is not positive, return
`inconclusive`.
Split each coordinate interval into its nonempty strictly negative and
strictly positive portions, plus the singleton $\{0\}$ when it contains zero.
Use the closures of the strictly signed portions as interval enclosures; form
their Cartesian products for the quadrant pieces, and handle products with an
axis singleton separately. Omit empty pieces. These finitely many pieces
cover the rectangle, with quadrant closures allowed to overlap their axis
pieces. On a quadrant where the denominator interval excludes zero, use
$$\operatorname{Arg}(x+iy)= \begin{cases} \arctan(y/x),&x>0,\ y>0,\\ -\arctan((-y)/x),&x>0,\ y<0,\\ \pi-\arctan(y/(-x)),&x<0,\ y>0,\\ -\pi+\arctan((-y)/(-x)),&x<0,\ y<0. \end{cases}$$
Write this call's fixed interval as $P_N=[p_-,p_+]$ and form the exact
dyadic sector intervals
$$S_{\rm I}=[0,p_+/2],\qquad S_{\rm II}=[p_-/2,p_+],\qquad S_{\rm III}=[-p_+,-p_-/2],\qquad S_{\rm IV}=[-p_+/2,0].$$
For every ratio-based quadrant piece, obtain its finite real arctangent
enclosure by the real rules above; propagate any non-finite result. Form the
full argument interval $A$ in the displayed quadrant formula by exact
rational endpoint arithmetic, using this same $P_N$ for each occurrence of
$\pi$. Before final outward conversion or hull formation, replace $A$ by
$J=A\cap S_q$, where $q$ is that piece's quadrant. Compute the intersection
by exact endpoint maxima and minima. If it is empty, return `inconclusive`
with the piece and status `empty-argument-intersection`; do not omit the
piece. If the denominator interval has a zero endpoint, use $J=S_q$
instead of a ratio formula.

For an interval $J=[a,b]$ produced by either branch, apply the same final
conversion $H(J)=[\operatorname{rd}(a),\operatorname{ru}(b)]$ in the selected
format. Perform this conversion after intersection for a ratio branch and
after selecting $S_q$ for a coarse branch. Finite subnormal endpoints are
accepted; an overflow returns `overflow` with the piece. On the positive
imaginary axis use $H(P_N/2)$, on the negative imaginary axis use
$H(-P_N/2)$, and on the positive real axis use $H([0,0])$. The initial domain
check excludes the origin and negative real axis, so these are all remaining
axis cases.

On each piece enclose $\ln\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}$ using the real operations and
evaluator, and combine it with the converted argument interval into a
rectangle. If every piece is finite, take the coordinatewise hull of all
piece rectangles. If any piece, conversion or branch is unresolved, return
its status and piece without forming a partial hull.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and
$Y\subseteq Y'$, then the computed set enclosure of $X\circ Y$ is contained
in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Every finite interval returned for a requested real output node by
[[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] on an input interval in the
domain of $\exp$, $\ln$, $\sqrt{\phantom{x}}$, $\arctan$, $\sin$, $\cos$, or
$\tan$ contains the exact range of the corresponding function on that
interval. For the same typed DAG and designated real output node, if all
input intervals are nested coordinatewise, all constant enclosures are fixed,
and both calls use the same finite dyadic format and truncation index $N$,
then, whenever both calls return finite enclosures, the canonical branch-cell
and fixed-term construction makes the smaller domain's computed enclosure a
subset of the larger one's.
An unresolved fixed branch, pole, invalid domain or overflow returns its
stated non-finite status and carries no finite success claim.

For every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and real $T$, the extension in [[def-boys-function-and-coulomb-auxiliary-recurrence]] satisfies
$$0<F_m(T)\le\frac1{2m+1},\qquad F_m(0)=\frac1{2m+1},$$
$$F_m(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-T)^k}{k!(2m+2k+1)},\qquad \frac{d}{dT}F_m(T)=-F_{m+1}(T).$$
The upper bound in the first display is asserted for $T\ge0$. For $T>0$ the function also satisfies
$$2T F_{m+1}(T)=(2m+1)F_m(T)-e^{-T},\qquad F_m(T)=\frac{\gamma(m+\tfrac12,T)}{2T^{m+1/2}}.$$
The complete Gamma factor at a half-integer is
$$\Gamma(m+\tfrac12)=\frac{(2m)!}{4^m m!}\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $m\ge0$, $T>0$, and let $I_m=[c_m-r_m,c_m+r_m]$ enclose $F_m(T)$ while $J=[c_e-r_e,c_e+r_e]$ encloses $e^{-T}$. The exact upward recurrence image for $F_{m+1}$ has radius at most
$$\frac{(2m+1)r_m+r_e}{2T},$$
and the exact downward recurrence image for $F_m$, from an interval of radius $r_{m+1}$ for $F_{m+1}$, has radius at most
$$\frac{2Tr_{m+1}+r_e}{2m+1}.$$
When both outward endpoint conversions are finite, the stored interval radius exceeds the exact-image radius by at most the mean of the two endpoint-rounding errors. If either endpoint conversion overflows, no finite recurrence interval or finite propagated estimate is asserted for that step. Iterating the displayed bounds gives valid finite error-amplification estimates over any requested order range for which every endpoint conversion is finite. Upward recurrence is undefined at $T=0$; direct values $F_m(0)=1/(2m+1)$ are exact.

A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval
$B=[a,b]$ with finite dyadic endpoints; for a complex value it is a nonempty
closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]]; the soundness of finite
arithmetic expression DAGs follows from
[[thm-outward-rounded-operations-are-isotone-and-dag-sound]]. Real elementary
function ranges use [[thm-real-elementary-range-enclosures]], and complex
exponential and principal-logarithm ranges use
[[thm-complex-elementary-range-enclosures]]. An operation that returns a
non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

derivations.claim: If an endpoint is zero, the internal rational is exactly $F_m(0)$ and its outward-rounded interval contains that value. Each positive-endpoint seed branch uses its own explicitly bound order $m\in\{0,M\}$. If the small-$T$ branch is used, [F3] encloses its Taylor sum by its first omitted term. If the positive midpoint branch is used, each exponential node is enclosed by [F7] and the quadrature remainder in [F4] encloses the integral. Thus every successful direct seed interval contains its Boys value.

In the large branch, [F6] encloses $\Gamma(m+\tfrac12)$ whenever its Gamma call succeeds. This target is real by the positive-real Euler integral and half-integer identity in [F8], so projection onto the real coordinate preserves its enclosure. The prescribed square roots and powers enclose the positive scaling factors by [F7], which also encloses $e^{-T}$, and [F5] bounds the omitted upper incomplete-gamma tail. Outward interval operations therefore produce a containing interval for $F_m(T)$.

For $T>0$, apply the exact recurrence identities [F8] to each previously enclosed order. The outward interval expression encloses the exact affine recurrence image, and [F9] bounds the stored radius, since the procedure forms each affine endpoint exactly rationally and adds both final outward-conversion errors. Induction over the finite order count proves every entry of either accepted candidate table contains its exact Boys value.

For $T_-\le T\le T_+$, [F8] makes $F_m$ decreasing, so its exact range lies between its endpoint values. The endpoint hull in [F1] therefore contains the entire range. The algorithm returns `success` only after the interval tests in [F2]; its other statuses make no success claim.

The algorithm visits only two endpoints and $M+1$ requested orders. Its refinement index is bounded by $W$; Taylor sums, midpoint panels and recurrence tables each have finite indices. More strongly, the shared counter is checked before every primitive operation and loop update, including all work inside Gamma and elementary subcalls. Every child receives the specified finite format/truncation inputs and the Gamma child additionally receives a finite work cap no larger than the remaining parent budget. Thus even a child whose complete construction would exceed that budget is interrupted with `inconclusive`; every branch returns a status after finitely many charged operations. No argument infers success from the size of a finite cap.

Let $a,b>0$, $A,B\in\mathbb R^3$, $p=a+b$, $\mu=ab/p$, and $P=(aA+bB)/p$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\exp(-a\|x-A\|_2^2)\exp(-b\|x-B\|_2^2)=\exp(-\mu\|A-B\|_2^2)\exp(-p\|x-P\|_2^2).$$
For any multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^3$, the polynomial factor $(x-A)^\alpha(x-B)^\beta$ is a finite polynomial in $x-P$ of total degree at most $|\alpha|+|\beta|$. Moreover, $P=(a/p)A+(b/p)B$ lies on the closed segment from $A$ to $B$.

In one dimension, let $g_i(x_A,a)=x_A^ie^{-ax_A^2}$ and $g_j(x_B,b)=x_B^je^{-bx_B^2}$, with $x_A=x-A$, $x_B=x-B$, $p=a+b$, $P=(aA+bB)/p$, and $K=e^{-ab(A-B)^2/p}$. There are unique coefficients $E_{ij}^t$ such that
$$g_i(x_A,a)g_j(x_B,b)=\sum_{t=0}^{i+j}E_{ij}^t\Lambda_t(x;p,P).$$
With $E_{00}^0=K$ and $E_{ij}^t=0$ outside $0\le t\le i+j$, they satisfy
$$E_{i+1,j}^t=\frac{E_{ij}^{t-1}}{2p}+(P-A)E_{ij}^t+(t+1)E_{ij}^{t+1},$$
$$E_{i,j+1}^t=\frac{E_{ij}^{t-1}}{2p}+(P-B)E_{ij}^t+(t+1)E_{ij}^{t+1}.$$
In three dimensions the pair expansion is the product of the three one-dimensional expansions, so it is a finite sum of $\Lambda_{tuv}$ with $0\le t\le\alpha_1+\beta_1$, $0\le u\le\alpha_2+\beta_2$, and $0\le v\le\alpha_3+\beta_3$.

Using $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ from [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], for $p>0$, $P\in\mathbb R^3$, and $t,u,v\in\mathbb N_0$, the **Hermite Gaussian** is
$$\Lambda_{tuv}(x;p,P)=\frac{\partial^{t+u+v}}{\partial P_1^t\partial P_2^u\partial P_3^v}\exp(-p\|x-P\|_2^2).$$
For $\eta>0$, $P,C\in\mathbb R^3$, and $n,t,u,v\in\mathbb N_0$, define the **Boys Coulomb auxiliary function**
$$R^n_{tuv}(\eta,P-C)=(-2\eta)^n\frac{\partial^{t+u+v}}{\partial P_1^t\partial P_2^u\partial P_3^v}F_n\!\left(\eta\|P-C\|_2^2\right).$$
Each derivative is an ordinary derivative of a smooth real function of the displayed center coordinates. For the Gaussian this follows from [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]] and repeated coordinatewise product and chain rules in [[lem-derivative-algebra-and-chain-rules]]. For the Boys composition, [[thm-boys-integral-identities-series-and-incomplete-gamma]] gives $F_n^{(k)}(T)=(-1)^kF_{n+k}(T)$ by iteration on the full real extension; these derivatives are continuous by its integral representation and compact-uniform domination. The chain rules therefore also apply when $P=C$, where the Boys argument is zero. The multi-index $(t,u,v)$ records derivative order and $n$ records Boys order; both are nonnegative integers.

For every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and real $T$, the extension in [[def-boys-function-and-coulomb-auxiliary-recurrence]] satisfies
$$0<F_m(T)\le\frac1{2m+1},\qquad F_m(0)=\frac1{2m+1},$$
$$F_m(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-T)^k}{k!(2m+2k+1)},\qquad \frac{d}{dT}F_m(T)=-F_{m+1}(T).$$
The upper bound in the first display is asserted for $T\ge0$. For $T>0$ the function also satisfies
$$2T F_{m+1}(T)=(2m+1)F_m(T)-e^{-T},\qquad F_m(T)=\frac{\gamma(m+\tfrac12,T)}{2T^{m+1/2}}.$$
The complete Gamma factor at a half-integer is
$$\Gamma(m+\tfrac12)=\frac{(2m)!}{4^m m!}\sqrt\pi.$$
$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt\pi.$$

Let $p>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$. If any component of $\alpha$ is odd, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=0.$$
If $\alpha_j=2k_j$ for $j=1,2,3$, then

derivations.claim: For $r>0$, the Gaussian integral and substitution $u=sr$ give $r^{-1}=(2/\sqrt\pi)\int_0^\infty e^{-s^2r^2}ds$. Completing the square in $x$ using [F1] gives a three-dimensional Gaussian integral $(\pi/(p+s^2))^{3/2}$ times $e^{-ps^2\|P-C\|^2/(p+s^2)}$. The substitution $t=s/\sqrt{p+s^2}$ maps $[0,\infty)$ monotonically onto $[0,1)$ and simplifies the remaining factor to $2\pi/p\int_0^1e^{-p\|P-C\|^2t^2}dt$, which is the stated base formula.

From [F4] and the chain rule, $\partial_{P_1}F_n(p\|P-C\|^2)=-2p(P_1-C_1)F_{n+1}(p\|P-C\|^2)$. Applying $\partial_{P_1}^t\partial_{P_2}^u\partial_{P_3}^v$ and the product rule to $(P_1-C_1)F_{n+1}$ produces one term $(P_1-C_1)R^{n+1}_{tuv}$ and $t$ terms $R^{n+1}_{t-1,u,v}$. Multiplying by the normalization $(-2p)^n$ yields the displayed recurrence; the same argument applies to the other coordinates.

For the two-center base, set $z=x-y$ and integrate first in $x$. Completing the square with [F1] gives $$\int_{\mathbb R^3}e^{-p\|x-P\|^2}e^{-q\|x-z-Q\|^2}dx=(\pi/(p+q))^{3/2}e^{-\eta\|z-(P-Q)\|^2}.$$ Absolute convergence [F6] justifies the change of variables and order of integration. Applying step 1.1 with exponent $\eta$ and center difference $P-Q$, then simplifying $(\pi/(p+q))^{3/2}(2\pi/\eta)$, gives $2\pi^{5/2}/(pq\sqrt{p+q})$ times the stated Boys value.

By [F6], differentiating either base integral with respect to its Gaussian centers is valid for every finite derivative order. Since $\Lambda_{tuv}$ is exactly the corresponding center derivative by [F3], the one-center Hermite Coulomb integral is $(2\pi/p)\partial_P^{tuv}F_0=(2\pi/p)R^0_{tuv}$. In the two-center case, derivatives in $Q$ act on $P-Q$ with a minus sign for each coordinate derivative; hence the Hermite integral is the base constant times $(-1)^{\tau+\nu+\phi}\partial_{P-Q}^{t+\tau,u+\nu,v+\phi}F_0$.

Substitute the finite expansions from [F2] into the one- and two-center integrals. Linearity makes the sums finite. The one-center Hermite formula from step 3.1 gives the stated nuclear formula, and the two-center formula from step 3.1 gives the displayed signed double sum. Complex contractions use conjugate-linear coefficients in the first pair exactly as in [F1]'s Coulomb form; the primitive formulas are real.

**Inputs.** A finite list of input basis contractions $\phi_a=\sum_{i=1}^{q_a}d_{ai}g_{ai}$, $1\le a\le n$, from [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], represented by finite dyadic intervals for real centers and positive exponents and finite dyadic intervals or complex rectangles for coefficients; a finite nuclear list $((C_\ell,w_\ell))_{\ell=1}^J$ whose centers and signed real weights are represented by finite dyadic intervals; a requested subset $\mathcal I\subseteq\{S,T,V,G\}$ of integral outputs (overlap, kinetic, nuclear attraction, and Coulomb); and Boolean energy and gradient requests, with a gradient request requiring an energy request. Require at least one requested output. Supply a positive integral tolerance $\varepsilon_I$ for every requested integral and for integrals used internally by an energy request; supply a positive energy tolerance $\varepsilon_E$ when energy is requested and, for a gradient request, an optional positive gradient tolerance defaulting to $\varepsilon_E$. An optional positive screening tolerance is allowed only for an energy request. Also supply finite positive integer work and precision caps $W,P$ and a dyadic format of precision $2\le p\le P$ with exponent bounds and fixed elementary truncation index $K\ge1$. A primitive request is the singleton-contraction case. An energy/gradient request additionally requires $n,r\ge1$, real primitive-contraction coefficients $d_{ai}$ and real nuclear data, real matrices $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times r},D\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$ given by dyadic boxes (exact matrices are singleton boxes), and uniform finite bounds $B\ge\sup\|C\|_F$, $M_D\ge\sup\|D\|_F$ from [[def-finite-gaussian-basis-variational-energy-and-gradient]]. Internal primitive labels $(a,i)$ are distinct from the input basis labels $a$; $C$ is a subsequent transform of the input basis.

**Outputs.** A status `success`, `inconclusive`, `domain`, or `range`; outward real intervals or complex rectangles for the integrals in $\mathcal I$; an energy interval when energy is requested; a gradient center and Frobenius gradient-error bound when gradient is requested; and a separately accumulated discarded-energy bound when screening is enabled. Success encloses every parameter value in the input boxes. No status declares an omitted integral zero.

**Finite calls and accounting.** Use [[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] for arithmetic. Every real elementary call means a typed DAG call to [[alg-certified-elementary-range-evaluation]] at the supplied format and $K$. Enclose $\pi$ by the $K$-term Machin/arctangent certificate in [[lem-trigonometric-identities-machin-and-range-reduction]], with exact rational tail endpoints before final outward conversion. A shared counter charges each conversion, comparison, loop update, arithmetic operation, recurrence update and summand, including every primitive operation executed by a child. Check the counter before executing an operation and interrupt any child at exhaustion. A required Boys call receives remaining work $R$ as its finite work cap, precision cap $P$, the same format and $K$, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_I/2$ and no relative request; its actual work is charged to the parent. A required child non-success on otherwise valid data or an intermediate overflow makes the current integral evaluation `inconclusive`; a rounded intermediate failing a domain certification on valid original data is also `inconclusive`. Return `range` only when a certified lower bound for a requested exact output component exceeds the largest finite magnitude of the format or a certified upper bound is below its negative. A mere overflow of a conservative intermediate or enclosure endpoint is not enough to claim `range`. Invalid original inputs return `domain`; cap exhaustion returns `inconclusive`. These choices are conservative and need not permit success under every cap or tolerance.

1. Validate the request specification, positive exponent lower endpoints, finite input boxes, indices in $\mathbb N_0^3$, supported format and positive tolerances/caps. Invalid original data return `domain`. If energy/gradient is requested, verify realness and dimensions and certify the norm bounds by outward Frobenius upper bounds on the complete boxes. If this sufficient norm test cannot certify the supplied bounds, return `inconclusive`; do not claim that an unknown represented matrix violates its bound. Form finite primitive-pair and quartet lists for the requested integrals and any energy/gradient dependencies, lexicographically. Include all shifted overlap pairs required by the kinetic raising/lowering formula; a negative index contributes zero.

For each ordered primitive pair with exponents $a,b$, indices $\alpha,\beta$ and centers $A,B$, compute $p=a+b$, $P=(aA+bB)/p$, and $K_{ab}=\exp(-ab\|A-B\|^2/p)$ by outward arithmetic and the real elementary call. The final table has $\prod_{j=1}^3(\alpha_j+\beta_j+1)$ entries; every intermediate table update is also charged. Compute overlap by the finite shifted polynomial expansion and the moments in [[lem-cartesian-gaussian-moments-and-parameter-derivatives]], and kinetic by [[thm-cartesian-gaussian-raising-lowering-and-kinetic-recurrences]]. Certified square roots and integer powers evaluate all half-integer factors in those moment formulas.

3. To evaluate an attraction primitive pair, put $L=|\alpha|+|\beta|$ and use exponent $\eta=p$ and center difference $P-C_{\rm nuc}$. A **certified enclosure** for a real value is a nonempty closed interval

closed rectangle $B=[a_1,b_1]+i[a_2,b_2]$ with finite dyadic endpoints. Its
radius is half its length in the real case and half its Euclidean diagonal in
the complex case; $d(B,0)$ is the Euclidean distance from $B$ to $0$.
An evaluator item declares whether its input is an exact dyadic point or a
dyadic interval/rectangle enclosure; a successful range result contains the
exact function image of every admissible point in an input enclosure. Constants
not exactly dyadic must be supplied with certified enclosing intervals or
rectangles.

The interval backend uses the endpoint operations in

arithmetic expression DAGs follows from

non-finite status supplies no finite enclosure claim.

A finite-budget evaluator receives a branch input enclosure wholly within
the stated domain, absolute tolerance $\varepsilon_a>0$, optional relative
tolerance $\varepsilon_r>0$, finite integer work and precision caps, and the
fixed format and truncation parameters required by the backend. Its result has
one of four statuses:

- `success`: the returned enclosure contains the exact requested value and its
  radius is at most $\varepsilon_a$. If $0\notin B$ and relative tolerance was
  requested, the evaluator may also report `relative_certified: true` only when
  $\operatorname{rad}(B)/d(B,0)\le\varepsilon_r$.
- `inconclusive`: the procedure exhausted a finite cap before its requested
  enclosure test passed.
- `domain`: the input is outside the stated branch domain, violates a stated
  parameter condition, or lies on a branch cut excluded by that branch.
- `range`: a certified finite enclosure cannot be represented in the requested
  output format; the procedure returns no unsound finite interval.

If a success enclosure contains $0$, it still supplies the stated absolute
bound, but it carries no relative-accuracy claim. The work and precision caps
do not imply that success occurs for every input.

For real intervals, complex rectangles or complex balls on which an operation
is defined, enlarging either input enclosure cannot shrink the computed
enclosure: for binary $\circ\in\{+,-,\times,\div\}$, if $X\subseteq X'$ and

in that of $X'\circ Y'$ whenever both are finite results and their domain
restrictions are preserved. The square-root enclosure is inclusion-isotone on
nonnegative intervals. Each finite ball operation in
[[def-outward-rounded-interval-and-ball-operations]] contains the exact ball
image. A `split-domain`, `entire`, `domain-error`, `overflow`, or
`inconclusive` status makes no finite claim. For a finite expression DAG
whose operation nodes all return finite enclosures, every exact node value
from every admissible input assignment belongs to its computed node
enclosure; in particular, the root enclosure contains the exact range. If any
node returns a non-finite status, no finite DAG enclosure is asserted.

Let $p>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$. If any component of $\alpha$ is odd, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=0.$$
If $\alpha_j=2k_j$ for $j=1,2,3$, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=\pi^{3/2}\prod_{j=1}^3\frac{(2k_j)!}{4^{k_j}k_j!\,p^{k_j+1/2}}.$$
For every $q\in\mathbb N_0$, differentiation with respect to $p$ is valid and
$$\frac{d^q}{dp^q}\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=(-1)^q\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|x\|_2^{2q}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx.$$

For $g_{\alpha,a,A}$ from [[def-cartesian-gaussian-primitives-and-contractions]], let $e_j$ be the $j$th coordinate vector. With terms having negative indices interpreted as zero,
$$\partial_{x_j}g_{\alpha,a,A}=\alpha_jg_{\alpha-e_j,a,A}-2ag_{\alpha+e_j,a,A},\qquad \partial_{A_j}g_{\alpha,a,A}=-\alpha_jg_{\alpha-e_j,a,A}+2ag_{\alpha+e_j,a,A}.$$
The second spatial derivative and kinetic operator are
$$\partial_{x_j}^2g_{\alpha,a,A}=\alpha_j(\alpha_j-1)g_{\alpha-2e_j,a,A}-2a(2\alpha_j+1)g_{\alpha,a,A}+4a^2g_{\alpha+2e_j,a,A},$$
$$-\frac12\Delta g_{\alpha,a,A}=\sum_{j=1}^3\left(-\frac{\alpha_j(\alpha_j-1)}2g_{\alpha-2e_j,a,A}+a(2\alpha_j+1)g_{\alpha,a,A}-2a^2g_{\alpha+2e_j,a,A}\right).$$
Consequently every kinetic integral of finite contractions is a finite linear combination of overlap integrals with these shifted multi-indices.

For every $m\in\mathbb N_0$ and real $T$, the extension in [[def-boys-function-and-coulomb-auxiliary-recurrence]] satisfies
$$0<F_m(T)\le\frac1{2m+1},\qquad F_m(0)=\frac1{2m+1},$$
$$F_m(T)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-T)^k}{k!(2m+2k+1)},\qquad \frac{d}{dT}F_m(T)=-F_{m+1}(T).$$
The upper bound in the first display is asserted for $T\ge0$. For $T>0$ the function also satisfies
$$2T F_{m+1}(T)=(2m+1)F_m(T)-e^{-T},\qquad F_m(T)=\frac{\gamma(m+\tfrac12,T)}{2T^{m+1/2}}.$$
The complete Gamma factor at a half-integer is
$$\Gamma(m+\tfrac12)=\frac{(2m)!}{4^m m!}\sqrt\pi.$$

For $p>0$, $P,C\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\eta=pq/(p+q)$ with $p,q>0$, the Hermite Coulomb auxiliaries of [[def-hermite-gaussian-coulomb-auxiliary-functions]] satisfy
$$R^n_{000}(p,P-C)=(-2p)^nF_n(p\|P-C\|^2),$$
$$R^n_{t+1,u,v}=(P_1-C_1)R^{n+1}_{tuv}+tR^{n+1}_{t-1,u,v},$$
with the corresponding coordinate formulas for increasing $u$ or $v$ and with negative-index terms zero. The one-center and two-center base Coulomb integrals are
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}\frac{e^{-p\|x-P\|^2}}{\|x-C\|}\,dx=\frac{2\pi}{p}F_0(p\|P-C\|^2),$$
$$\int\!\!\int\frac{e^{-p\|x-P\|^2}e^{-q\|y-Q\|^2}}{\|x-y\|}\,dy\,dx=\frac{2\pi^{5/2}}{pq\sqrt{p+q}}F_0(\eta\|P-Q\|^2).$$
For a primitive pair expansion $g_ag_b=\sum_{tuv}E_{ab}^{tuv}\Lambda_{tuv}$, the nuclear attraction integral is
$$V_C(g_a,g_b)=\frac{2\pi}{p}\sum_{tuv}E_{ab}^{tuv}R^0_{tuv}(p,P-C).$$
For two primitive pairs, with coefficients $E_{ab}$ and $E_{cd}$ and centers $P,Q$, the Coulomb integral is
$$G(g_a,g_b;g_c,g_d)=\frac{2\pi^{5/2}}{pq\sqrt{p+q}}\sum_{tuv}\sum_{\tau\nu\phi}\overline{E_{ab}^{tuv}}E_{cd}^{\tau\nu\phi}(-1)^{\tau+\nu+\phi}R^0_{t+\tau,u+\nu,v+\phi}(\eta,P-Q).$$
All sums are finite; the largest Boys order is bounded by the total polynomial degree in the participating primitives.

Let $a,b>0$, $A,B\in\mathbb R^3$, $p=a+b$, $\mu=ab/p$, and $P=(aA+bB)/p$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\exp(-a\|x-A\|_2^2)\exp(-b\|x-B\|_2^2)=\exp(-\mu\|A-B\|_2^2)\exp(-p\|x-P\|_2^2).$$

Let $n,r\ge1$ be integers, $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}$, $D\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$, $H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$, and $G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n\times n\times n}$. Define their transformed tensors by
$$H'_{pq}=\sum_{a,b=1}^n C_{ap}H_{ab}C_{bq},\qquad G'_{pqrs}=\sum_{a,b,c,d=1}^n C_{ap}C_{bq}C_{cr}C_{ds}G_{abcd},$$
for $1\le p,q,r,s\le r$. Define the finite **variational energy functional**
$$E(C;D,H,G)=\sum_{p,q=1}^r D_{pq}H'_{pq}+\frac12\sum_{p,q,r,s=1}^r D_{pq}D_{rs}G'_{pqrs}.$$
Its gradient $\nabla_C E$ is the ordinary Euclidean gradient with respect to the $nr$ real entries of $C$. The basis dimension is $n$, the contracted dimension is $r$, and for any finite matrix or tensor $A$, $\|A\|_F=(\sum |A_{i_1\ldots i_k}|^2)^{1/2}$, with the sum over all its entries. This is a finite algebraic functional; it assumes no Hartree–Fock, self-consistency, or minimizing-state postulate.

For perturbed integral tensors $\widetilde H,\widetilde G$, write $\widetilde E$ for the same functional with those tensors and the same fixed $C,D$. The word “variational” here names the finite coefficient functional only; no claim about a stationary point or physical energy is included.

Let $n,r\ge1$, $C\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}$ with $\|C\|_F\le B$, and $D\in\mathbb R^{r\times r}$ with $\|D\|_F\le M$. Suppose $|\widetilde H_{ab}-H_{ab}|\le\varepsilon_2$ and $|\widetilde G_{abcd}-G_{abcd}|\le\varepsilon_4$ for every entry. With the functional of [[def-finite-gaussian-basis-variational-energy-and-gradient]],
$$|\widetilde E-E|\le MrnB^2\varepsilon_2+\frac12M^2r^2n^2B^4\varepsilon_4,$$
and
$$\|\nabla_C\widetilde E-\nabla_CE\|_F\le2nrBM\varepsilon_2+2n^2r^2B^3M^2\varepsilon_4.$$

Let $a,b>0$, $A,B\in\mathbb R^3$, $p=a+b$, $\mu=ab/p$, and $P=(aA+bB)/p$. Then for every $x\in\mathbb R^3$,
$$\exp(-a\|x-A\|_2^2)\exp(-b\|x-B\|_2^2)=\exp(-\mu\|A-B\|_2^2)\exp(-p\|x-P\|_2^2).$$
For any multi-indices $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^3$, the polynomial factor $(x-A)^\alpha(x-B)^\beta$ is a finite polynomial in $x-P$ of total degree at most $|\alpha|+|\beta|$. Moreover, $P=(a/p)A+(b/p)B$ lies on the closed segment from $A$ to $B$.

Let $p>0$ and $\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^3$. If any component of $\alpha$ is odd, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=0.$$
If $\alpha_j=2k_j$ for $j=1,2,3$, then
$$\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=\pi^{3/2}\prod_{j=1}^3\frac{(2k_j)!}{4^{k_j}k_j!\,p^{k_j+1/2}}.$$
For every $q\in\mathbb N_0$, differentiation with respect to $p$ is valid and
$$\frac{d^q}{dp^q}\int_{\mathbb R^3}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx=(-1)^q\int_{\mathbb R^3}\|x\|_2^{2q}x^\alpha e^{-p\|x\|_2^2}\,dx.$$

The Gram matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&S\\S&1\end{pmatrix}$, whose characteristic polynomial is $(1-\lambda)^2-S^2$, so its eigenvalues are $1\pm S$. At $a=b$, $S=1$ and the lower eigenvalue is zero.
